newsitem.title: JAPAN: TOCOM says to list crude or gasoline in 1999.
newsitem.headline: TOCOM says to list crude or gasoline in 1999.

text.p: The Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) said on Wednesday it plans to list either crude oil or gasoline in 1999 as its first-ever energy futures contract.
"At the moment, we consider crude and gasoline as the most promising futures contracts," Mitsuhiro Onosato, general manager of TOCOM's planning department told reporters.
"As for type of crude, it is most likely to be either WTI (West Texas Intermediate) or Brent," he said.
The news conference heralded the completion of what is now the fifth report on the possibility of listing energy futures in Japan.
The latest report, as well as four earlier versions, was compiled by private think-tank Mitsubishi Research Institute for TOCOM.
The previous report, put out in February 1996, put forth gasoline as the leading candidate for the first energy futures.
But a government decision earlier this year to relax foreign exchange controls in 1998 has made the listing of dollar-denominated crude futures contracts a realistic option.

Onosato said possible crude futures on TOCOM are expected to attract enough market participants, despite low liquidity of Brent futures on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), because of ample local funds .
"Abundant local funds and investors who are willing to take risks are necessary for any new futures to take off," he said.
"That's what Japan has, and Singapore may not," he said.

Some regional traders say Brent crude futures trading on SIMEX is slow because the majority of physical crude is traded in London time, making the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE)'s Brent futures contracts a viable hedging mechanism for crude dealers in Asia.
SIMEX's Brent market rarely achieves daily volumes of more than two hundred lots, while the IPE trades 40,000 to 50,000 lots each day.
Onosato also said listing Brent futures is not likely to incur conflicts with SIMEX, which has exclusive rights to list Brent contracts during Asian business hours under an agreement with IPE.
He added that TOCOM's contract would also differ from SIMEX in that it would not offer a mutual offset accord, in which positions opened on the SIMEX can be closed on the IPE and vice versa.
"We have no intentions to strike a mutual offset agreement with IPE," he said.
However, he said he would like to have talks with IPE and NYMEX this year or the next to iron out any potential problems.
